utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-33-A, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, please. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Prosecution this afternoon is Norman Farrell, Mr. Mathias Marcussen, and Nicola Bonfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the appellant?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Nenad Petrusic. I am representing the Defence of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. General Krstic, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? There's no need for you to stand up to answer. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Farrell, we've got a very large status report which you filed on the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that sort of the agenda for the hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic and the Prosecution met this afternoon, earlier on, and there's some information I can update you with, if you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: -- now, at this point. If I can -- it may be easiest just simply to refer to the status report, if you have it in front of you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Page 6 of the status report, paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: These are the remaining issues to be done by the Prosecution. At the bottom of page 6, following after paragraph 15, is a box, and I'll just walk you through that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The first is some outstanding disclosure that was to be disclosed within ten days. That has taken place and was couriered to Mr. Petrusic on the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the first box?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's the first box, Your Honour, where it says "Description: Disclosure of a few documents."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Those were just some remaining matters which have been subsequently disclosed. The second box, which is the -- relates to post-judgement material that, as a result of the Defence's invocation of Rule 66(B), the Prosecution will bring a motion to the Court asking to withhold certain documents that they would normally get under 66(B), because of security or other concerns, that would fall under 66(C). So it's simply -- it's material which may fall under Rule 66(B), but the Prosecution will ask that it be permitted to withhold it, with the Court's agreement. That motion, we had indicated, would be filed within ten days, so it should have been filed today, Your Honour. I've informed the Defence, and I apologise: We won't be able to file that probably for another seven days, but it's pretty much done. So that remains outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've no doubt become aware, have you, that in seven days' time I'll be on home leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I wasn't completely aware of that. I'll try and get it done before then. But in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, no, because I should imagine that Rule 66(C) does not fall within the remit of a Pre-Appeal Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That would be true. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I did deal with it once in a trial but it was with the agreement of the other members of the Trial Chamber. I made a ruling under 66(C) by myself, but I think this would have to be with the approval of the other Judges of the Appeals Chamber, and so far as I can see from past experience, it is unlikely to be devolved upon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: This may cause some difficulty with the anticipated scheduling if this matter then isn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. No, no, because, unfortunately, I've had to divulge where I'm going to be, and there's a means of communication which no doubt I will be pestered with over the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My apologies. Regarding the third -- the third item, the third box, if I may. This relates to material that is -- was in the possession of the Prosecution pre-judgement, and as you recall, counsel for the appellant had asked to be provided with all material that falls under certain categories pre-judgement for the purpose of their review to see whether there was any Rule 68 material which was withheld by the Prosecution. I've spoken with Mr. Petrusic, and I leave it for him to confirm. I think this is a matter we can resolve ourselves. There's one matter that I have to get back to Mr. Petrusic on, and it's my understanding that Mr. Petrusic has undertaken to accept the assurances of the Prosecution with respect to those documents. If that's his understanding of our discussion this afternoon, I think this third item will not have to be brought by motion before the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The confidential sources, is that a Rule 70 point or is it some other confidential basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No. For those ones, it would be the equivalent of Rule 66(C) where material can be withheld because of security concerns or investigative concerns. It's more the investigative concerns. The difficulty we had in characterising this was that Rule 66(B) wasn't invoked at trial. The reason we're giving them was just on the agreement between counsel for the purposes of them being able to successfully argue their appeal, or at least bringing it. So there's no applicable Rule that we have to seek the order of the Court to withhold it. There's no obligation to disclose it. So that was the dilemma we found ourselves in. We had material that the Defence wanted access to from trial. We agreed to disclose most of the intercepts and the other things from trial, but there are some that come from sources that are for investigative purposes the Prosecution doesn't wish to disclose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But what is the resolution of the tension between Rule 66(C) and Rule 68? Is there some way of disclosing material in a redacted form?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: For anything -- for material, for example, in the one -- the category above, which would be that which on appeal should be disclosed to the appellant under 66(B) but may be from what we would call an investigative source, in those circumstances, we've undertaken with Mr. Petrusic to make efforts if there is anything in there that is Rule 68, we would find a way to get it to them. And the ones that we're asking you to -- the Court, under Rule 66(C), not to give would be matters that fall under 66(B), material for the preparation of the defence but are not Rule 68. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Nevertheless, material which is relevant to the preparation of the defence includes material which is relevant to the preparation of an appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. Preparation of the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. And it would include matters which were relevant. I must say the Rule 66(C) matter that I dealt with was of very peripheral nature. There was quite a body of it, but it was all quite peripheral, and it had been sought specifically by the accused as part of a much larger bundle of documents that had been seized somewhere. So I didn't have to worry about this, because there was clearly nothing in it which was relevant to anything which had been raised by the accused as an issue in the trial and appeared to be unlikely to be relevant to any matter he could raise in the trial. But I'm a little worried where something falls clearly within 66(B), which is material you have, which would be relevant to the preparation of the appeal simply because it was on a confidential basis if there was some way of disclosing it. Now, from what you've said, you're obviously attempting to get around that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The Rule 68 material we will certainly find a way around the problem and go back to the source if it's necessary, find a way and disclose it without -- in redacted form if possible. For the confidential sources that do not provide -- or sensitive investigative sources - "confidential sources" may be an improper word - investigative sources which do not provide Rule 68 but, as you've indicated, provide Rule 66(B) material, for preparation of the case, we do have some concerns about disclosing them because of the very sensitive nature of the information, and it's those ones which we respectfully submit are rather peripheral. 66(B) also includes inculpatory material. So if their statement is purely inculpatory but it is material to the preparation of the defence in the sense that it relates directly to his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it would be relevant under 66(B) if the Prosecution proposed to use it as part of its case. Well, that's hardly relevant on the appeal unless it's something to do with rebuttal evidence under Rule 115. But Rule 66(B) also deals with copies of Prosecution witness statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- when a decision has been made to call those witnesses. Well, that's obviously not applicable to an appeal. "... copies of statements of all witnesses" -- wait a minute. I'm looking at the wrong part of it. "... intended for use by the Prosecution as evidence at trial, material for preparation of the defence or obtained from or belonged to the accused." Now, you suggest, do you, that that phrase "material to the preparation of the appeal" would not include material or need not include material which is purely inculpatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I understood you to be saying, that this material, some of it, is purely inculpatory, and you don't want to disclose it because it's going to be embarrassing to your investigators, and if it is purely inculpatory, there's no need for it to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, in summary there. There may be a reason under 66(C) which overrides evidence though potentially discloseable under Rule 66(B) it's inculpatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it depends upon whether you're going to use it or attempt to use it. And if you're going to use it, you've got to disclose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But it may be in a certain redacted form. That's the way I see the relationship between (B) and (C), paragraphs (B) and (C) of Rule 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution will file the motion and for some of the material we will only be seeking redacted form. For some of the material if we're not, we'll set out exactly why, and if the Court doesn't accept that, then we'll, of course, file it based on whatever protective measures the Court so orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that seems to be the logical way of dealing with it, but some of the statements you make in your submissions had me worried. For example, in paragraph 11: "The Prosecution is under no obligation to disclose this material under Rule 66(B) as it was available during trial."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: There's been no 66(B) invoked during trial, and the material that they're asking for in relation to pre-judgement material, they have no right to. There's pre-judgement material, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. But as it was available during the trial. Available to whom? To the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. The decision in the Rwanda case of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Let's get it straight, because this is hardly clear. Are you saying that because it was available to the Defence during trial --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If they invoked Rule 66(B) during trial, it would have been available to them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If they had invoked Rule 66(B).

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that they are faced with the proposition that in order to get something which would normally be available, made available to them under 66(B), because the Prosecution were going to use it or whatever, they have to say, "All right. Well, we'll invoke reciprocal disclosure in order to get it."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Under the Rules, there's a regime for this matter, and if they do not invoke Rule 66(B) during trial, they can't invoke Rule 66(B) on appeal and ask for it to be somehow bounced back to the trial stage when they didn't invoke reciprocal disclosure. That's the decision in the Rutaganda Appeals Chamber decision. And my understanding is they said Rule 66(B) invoked on appeal means that any material that's come into the possession of the Prosecution post-judgement and doesn't apply to pre-judgement material. So that paragraph refers to their request to material which was available at trial if they invoked Rule 66(B) but didn't and have now asked us for any material that falls in a particular category of documents. And the Prosecution's position is if it's Rule 68, it should have been disclosed during trial, and if not, it be disclosed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're speaking to, I'm afraid, a non-French speaker, and Rutaganda is only available in French, as I understand it, and I have no idea what it says. So that this didn't make sense, but now it is starting to make sense. That is the problem, of course, with the Rwanda Appeals Chamber, that so much of it is in French, and you're lucky to get an English translation of it for something like two or three years. But thank you for explaining that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: At least, that's the position of the Prosecution. I may have read it wrong, but that's my understanding of the decision, at least the decision appended of Judge Shahabuddeen and Judge Jorda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Well, then, the next stage of your box.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The fourth one on the way, of them, is Rule 66(B), post-judgement, ongoing. Just to inform you that there is material which has come into the possession of the Prosecution since -- on November 5th -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. If I may back up. On November 5, Mr. Petrusic attended in The Hague and received reciprocal disclosure. Since that date, there has been material that's come into our possession, or audiotapes, which we now have recorded, which we will be disclosing to Mr. Petrusic. It's not a large item - sorry - a large number of items, but I just wanted to tell you that there are, I guess, about 15 items that we're reviewing. I don't know whether they all fit under Rule 66(B) or not. They've just come in from ongoing investigation. They will be reviewed and disclosed as soon as possible, as required under Rule 66(B), to Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, then you complain that there's been inadequate disclosure -- reciprocal disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I can address that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrusic met with us today -- and once again, I'll let Mr. Petrusic address this issue if I'm incorrect. He has provided a certain amount of reciprocal disclosure today, a small amount, but he's demonstrated that he brought what he could at this point in time. He's indicated that for certain other matters, he would try and get them as soon as possible; and for the recently disclosed ones, on November 5th, it's completely understandable that he may not be in a position at this stage to say which ones he's going to use in Court and which would therefore fall under Rule 66(C). He's informed us that he will attempt to give that to us as soon as possible. The Prosecution have no objections with Mr. Petrusic's suggestions for reciprocal disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm a little concerned -- I'm sorry. I didn't wait for the translation to finish. I'm a little concerned by the statement that is made in paragraph 18. It says: "It is the Prosecution's position that the source of the material which falls within Rule 67(C) is not determinative of a party's reciprocal disclosure obligations." Now, is that another shorthand statement? What about, for example, Rule 70?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It may be the way it's worded, and that would be my mistake. This is in relation -- the Defence had indicated that they didn't have to provide any Rule 66(C) material to the Prosecution, under Rule 66(C), if they got it from the Prosecution. They said that, well, we don't need to provide you -- and I don't want to paraphrase. I'll let Mr. Petrusic state it. My understanding of the correspondence we had with the Defence was that they said: Well, if we got it from you as a result of disclosure at any point in time, then, under 66(C), we don't have to identify those documents which the Defence intends to use as evidence on the appeal. And our position was: Well, the source of the documents, being their coming from the Prosecution or their coming from your own investigations, can't be the determinative issue as to what you have to identify under Rule 67(C). The Prosecution is entitled to see the documents that he intends to use as evidence at the trial. And that statement is not meant to be a generic statement, and if it is, that's my fault. It's meant to be a statement that since the Defence received material from the Prosecution as a result of disclosure at any point in time, that doesn't mean that it relieves them of the Rule 66(C) obligation. That was the purpose of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you don't really want them to serve you with all of the material which you've served them. What you are really after is the identification of the material they wish to rely upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And if they do that, it would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. The original -- yes. The original discussion was that they didn't -- it wasn't required because they received it from us. I think Mr. Petrusic and I have discussed this issue. I don't think there's any -- this statement doesn't cause any more concern between us, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It certainly did cause me some concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, thank you for raising it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. What next?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Those are the issues outstanding, as far as I'm Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. aware, between the appellant and the Prosecution respondent in relation to disclosure matters. There are two other matters that I informed -- two or three other matters I informed Mr. Petrusic I would get back to him on. I can speak with him after the Status Conference, as I have the answers for him, but they don't affect the matter presently before Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you do complain, for example, that there is no submissions made by the appellant concerning the failure to comply with Rule 68 at the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I was going to address this if we reached the issue of the scheduling of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we're going to get that eventually, so let's discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Prosecution's submission, there are two, I would think, two motions that will be coming your way, and our way. One --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, of course, any material which they did not have at trial, and that may even include some of the material that they claim they didn't get because of the violation of Rule 68. It's my understanding that there is an independent ground of appeal, which is that the trial was unfair because Rule 68 was violated. Now, under the jurisprudence of our Tribunal, you don't necessarily need to bring that in under 115 to prove the unfairness of the proceedings, and that if that's a separate matter and a separate ground of appeal on the material that was not disclosed, or allegedly not disclosed at trial, then that becomes a separate motion -- or it probably would be a supplementary to the appeal brief on the ground of appeal that there was a violation of Rule 68 and now they have the evidence they intend to rely on to support it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are certainly made aware in courtroom I of when the translation finishes, and I'm sorry if I've been travelling too quickly for them. There is a ground of appeal that the trial is not fair, and as I understand from my brief reading of it, is that they rely upon the fact there was a failure to comply with Rule 68. So there's a ground of appeal directed solely to that. Now, in order to prove the non-compliance with Rule 68, as I understand it, they're going to rely upon the material which has since been disclosed of a pre-judgement time frame. So I'm not sure that they have to actually tender that in order to establish their ground of appeal. They just produce it. It's not being tendered necessarily as additional evidence in the trial. It doesn't seem to me to fit within Rule 115. So they can say: If we had had this at the trial, we could have followed up all manner of lines of inquiry. And one would hope that they might be able to give us more detail of what they would have expected to find. But I don't see that as Rule 115 material. It's not being put forward as additional evidence in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I think we're in agreement here. That's why I was distinguishing between the two, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But nevertheless, we're going to have to deal with Rule 115. Now, may I raise this with you: Because of Rule 6, the old form of Rule 115 presently applies in this appeal, which permits a motion for fresh evidence 15 days before the day of hearing. Now, I'm sure that those of us who have had to deal with a few appeals recently would understand that that's a totally inadequate time frame, and if Mr. Petrusic wants some chapter and verse, I'll give it to him. And I propose to invite you to make an application under Rule 127, which is required to be by way of motion - an oral motion would be sufficient - that that time be changed. My contemplation at the moment is, subject to anything which Mr. Petrusic may have put forward, is to order any motion under 115 to be filed within the first week of term next year, on the basis that the appeal will be heard sometime middle/late February. That should, I hope, give the Prosecution sufficient time to deal with it, and also to find any rebuttal material. The Rule itself, Rule 115, I think was drafted by Judges who didn't quite contemplate what was going to be involved in it, because, as it presently stands, the Prosecution doesn't have to put forward its rebuttal material until the Appeals Chamber rules that it's admissible. And it is not really a very comfortable way of doing it, especially as the Rule, as it presently stands, says that the decision on the admissibility may be made after the hearing of the appeal. Now, I don't want there to be any argument available to anybody if I simply just change the timing, but if the Prosecution makes an oral motion that it be changed, I will certainly give it very careful consideration, subject to anything Mr. Petrusic has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In light of the timing that's been proposed for the possible hearing of the appeal, and in light of our experience in other cases, we would certainly request for a variation of the time limit from that which is required in the Rules. I think it's fair to say that 15 days would cause a somewhat onerous burden on the Prosecution, and probably a worse one on the Court when we file our material. If that's possible, the filing of the Defence material by the first week of January, and a reasonable period of time thereafter for the Prosecution to review the additional evidence, subject to what material is filed, of course. If it's more towards the end of February, I think the Prosecution could find a way to deal with this matter, and if that's -- if the Court grants the motion under 127, that may be satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What I would do is to suggest to both parties that if there are any problems in the preparation during the months of January or February for hearing the appeal, they can always have a Status Conference called so that can be sorted out, although I'm glad to see that so far counsel have managed to sort out most of these things themselves. But you can always have a Status Conference renewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Or a new Status Conference called. I will be back to start work again yet on the 7th of January -- the 6th of January. Is there anything else you want to raise, Mr. Farrell?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, Mr. Petrusic, do you want to say anything about what has been said so far by Mr. Farrell?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when discussing what my learned friend has said about his obligations from the status report of the 15th of November, this afternoon we reached agreement, and I think that we shall be able to relieve the Chamber of any obligations in this respect. An issue has been touched upon that I wish to mention, and that is the Rule 115 obligation of the Defence and the old Rules, before July, which applied. What I am concerned about is the voluminous amount of material received under Rule 68, both before and after the judgement, and the material received during reciprocal disclosure. I have looked through a considerable amount of this material, and I have to say that I'm finding highly relevant material which I cannot simply pass over due to lack of time, conditionally speaking. Let me be quite clear. I'm not asking for any additional time, but, as I told the Prosecutor today, I am prepared to file the submission, as you said, in the first week of January, and I believe this can be done on the 9th of January. I don't know whether that's a Sunday or not. But the amount of material is really enormous. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. But the 9th of January is a Thursday, as I understand it, so you'll be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, when making my plans, I did look at the calendar, and I did pay attention to that. So it might be in the middle of the week, maybe on Friday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We can make it the 10th, if you like, Mr. Petrusic. I don't want to press you on this unfairly, but you understand that I'm going to extend the time before the hearing of the appeal, that this material has to be filed and the application to give the Prosecution sufficient time to respond to it before the hearing of the appeal. Unfortunately, we've become rather painfully aware of the inadequacies of the 15 days that were provided for in the Rule. It is almost impossible for the Prosecution to respond and, therefore, completely impossible for the Appeals Chamber to be fully aware of the material at the time of the hearing of the appeal. If you think that you need longer, I will certainly listen to what you want to say, but whatever happens, it's going to have to be a period of at least six weeks, I think, between when you file it and when we can have the appeal. I also want to draw your attention to a recent amendment, further recent amendment to 115. It was in October. And this was also inserted as a consequence of the enormous problems that the Appeals Chamber has found in understanding what this additional material relates to in many cases. I'm sure the Prosecution has had a similar difficulty. Rule 115 presently provides that: "The motion to present the additional evidence shall clearly identify with precision the specific finding of fact made by the Trial Chamber to which the additional evidence is directed." Now, it may be very obvious, certainly to the appellant, what that fact is, but sometimes when you get a huge bundle of material it's difficult for people in a -- who receive it to work out what it's meant to be relevant to and that the order that you file your motion will include in it, I'm afraid, an obligation which is now imposed by that Rule. This question of additional evidence has assumed alarmingly great proportions of our time in appeals through no fault of anybody, really. It's the sudden disclosure by some governments of material which they should have disclosed a long time ago, and it's in the interests of justice for all concerned, even for the Prosecutor, that these matters be sorted out properly, and without the assistance of that identification of the findings of fact in which each document is meant to relate, it is enormously time-consuming, frustrating, and unnecessary for the Appeals Chamber to have to go looking for it themselves. So does that affect when you think you'll be ready to get your motion on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I addressed you previously, I said that in view of everything I have done so far, the materials I have looked at and the evidence I have identified, and knowing the amount of material I still have to go through, I hope and expect to be ready or, rather, to file my motion or my submission on the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you have any particular trouble, you can always seek an agreement from the Prosecution for an extension of time. I'm not quite sure who is going to be acting as the Pre-Appeal Judge during my absence, but if you do get into trouble, then you should make an application to the Appeals Chamber and somebody will be there to hear it. But I imagine, bearing in mind the degree of cooperation that has so far been exhibited by both counsel, that you should be able to sort it out between yourselves, and when I return to work, no doubt you will be able to present to me some sort of an agreed statement as to what has happened and what alterations should be made to any Scheduling Order that's made. I think we understand your problems, having been through them ourselves in a few appeals so far, and we don't want to place any unfair pressure on you. Our only concern is that this appeal should be heard at its earliest date which is reasonable in the circumstances. So if I order you to file any application under Rule 115 by the 10th of January, that order will be made on the understanding that you can approach us or the Prosecution if you are having trouble complying with it. Now, the other matter raised by the Prosecution related to your complaint of a non-compliance with Rule 68 during the course of the trial. It would be preferable, if not necessary, for you to identify in advance of the hearing the particular material which you now have which you say the absence of it has prejudiced you during the course of the trial. It's a point which is very much bound up with the additional evidence that you will be tendering, I should think, but there may be some material that you will rely upon not having had at the trial which caused you a particular prejudice and that will be relevant to that ground of appeal, but your submissions at the moment are understandably missing that particular detail. Would you be able to provide that particular detail also by the 10th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is precisely what I'm referring to, an all-inclusive submission referring both to the material withheld during the trial and the material disclosed after the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That, if I may say so, is a very sensible approach. Thank you. Now, is there anything else you want to do by way of -- to say by way of answer to Mr. Farrell or any other point you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I think all these issues have already been resolved and that the remainder will be resolved in the forthcoming period in the way stated by Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much indeed. Oh, I should ask is there anything you want to raise under Rule 65, the Status Conference Rule, by way of problems your client may be having?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problems, I would say, are constant and permanent. Mostly it's a matter of my client's health, the possible need for surgery. And I shall talk about this to representatives of the Registry, so I think there will be no need to put this forward at a hearing under Rule 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Rule 65 only gives you the opportunity of raising it if you've got nowhere with the Registry, but I suggest you deal with them first, and then if there is any further problem, I think your next avenue of appeal is to the President. But anyway, thank you very much for raising it. I've certainly heard what you've had to say about General Krstic's problems, which we all, I think, understand, and we hope that they will be looked after. Now, Mr. Farrell, assuming that you get the documents on the 10th of January, what sort of period have you got in mind for responding to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It's hopeful that in three to four weeks we may be in a position. I've asked Mr. Petrusic, under Rule 67(C), to provide the documents in advance, which may assist us to get a jump-start on some of this material, but it will depend primarily on the volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope it will be shorter than three to four weeks. I understand your difficulty as well, but if you have got the material in advance, if we are going to fix a hearing date towards the end of February, it will have to be much shorter than three to four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I guess it will depend on the material. I mean, if both are coming in on the 10th, there will be a certain amount of new material which is part of the Rule 68 ground of appeal supplementary material, and 115 material. Both have to be addressed within the same time frame. It's a little tight within three weeks, depending on the volume, to be able to address both of those, but we'll certainly endeavour to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, is there any point other than making the order for the filing of the Rule 115 material by the 10th of January? Is there any point in making any further orders at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I think one possibility I thought of, though I think, in fairness, Mr. Petrusic has indicated the time frame he can work under, and I respect that, but only other possibility is the Rule 68 material is not additional evidence and is supplementary to his ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, he's going to do that by the 10th of January as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But what I'm concerned about, and what the senior legal officer will be asking me later, is the hearing date.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm hopeful that towards the end of February we can make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm only wondering whether it's wise to make an order which may have to be changed at short notice, whereas after the 10th of January, you may be in a better position to be able to give a more definite idea, and whilst we can pencil in a hearing date at the end of February, which we'll notify the parties about, I think it's rather unwise me making orders if they've got to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I understand. I'm sorry. You're absolutely correct. I think we would be willing to work towards the date at the end of February. We will inform you within a few days after receiving the material the time frame that we think we can operate under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that would be the best way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to say in reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I'm very grateful to counsel on both sides for the cooperation they're showing with each other. It seems to me that there has to be an exception to the rule somewhere. This case is it. It's an appeal where counsel actually speak to each other. It's very good to see. Thank you very much. I will now adjourn.
